name: Architecture and Engineering
blurb: The boundaries that hold when detection misses: least privilege, egress control, agent identity, circuit breakers, and blast-radius limits enforced by machinery.

topics.body: Because injection cannot be filtered away, the durable defenses are architectural. Give the model the least privilege the task needs, require human approval before consequential actions such as sending, paying, or deleting, and constrain outbound network paths so a hijacked model has nowhere to exfiltrate to. Designs that separate a privileged planner from a quarantined reader, so the model that touches untrusted content never holds the authority to act, contain the blast radius even when the injection lands. The test of an AI architecture is not whether injection is possible but what the worst injected instruction could actually accomplish.
topics.name: Prompt Injection
topics.blurb: Direct and indirect prompt injection: how instructions hidden in content hijack model behavior, documented attacks, and current defenses.

topics.body: The architectural rule for jailbreaks is the same as for injection: refusal must not be the only barrier. A model talked out of its safety training should still hit authorization walls, egress limits, and human approval gates before anything consequential happens. If the only thing standing between a jailbreak and a harmful outcome is the model saying no, the architecture has already failed.
topics.name: Jailbreaks
topics.blurb: Techniques that bypass model safety training, and how labs measure and patch against them.

topics.body: Training and fine-tuning infrastructure is a production security boundary, not a research convenience. Version and hash training data snapshots so what a model learned from is reconstructable, isolate training environments from general development, sign artifacts at each pipeline stage, and record lineage so that when a dataset is later found poisoned, every downstream model it touched can be identified and retrained rather than guessed at.
topics.name: Model and Data Poisoning
topics.blurb: Corrupting training data or model weights to plant backdoors and biases, and the research on detecting it.

topics.body: The architectural answer to registry risk is an internal one: a curated, access-controlled model and dataset registry that mirrors approved external artifacts after scanning and signature verification, with admission control so production systems can only load from it. Namespace-reuse and typosquatting attacks against public registries are documented; an internal registry converts that entire attack class into a single controlled ingestion point.
topics.name: AI Supply Chain Attacks
topics.blurb: Compromised models, datasets, and packages upstream: malicious model files, dependency attacks, opaque fourth-party model chains, AI bills of materials, and registry integrity.

topics.body: Authorization has to happen at retrieval time, per user, not at the model. A shared index over documents with mixed sensitivity turns the model into a confused deputy that reads with its own broad permissions and answers to everyone. Segmenting stores by classification, enforcing the caller's entitlements in the retrieval layer, and keeping high-sensitivity corpora out of general-purpose assistants entirely are the designs that make leakage structurally hard rather than behaviorally discouraged.
topics.name: Data Leakage
topics.blurb: Training data extraction, membership inference, and models revealing what they should not.

topics.body: Weight protection is infrastructure discipline: encrypted storage, hardware-backed key custody, tightly scoped access with hardware MFA for the handful of roles that genuinely need it, egress monitoring on the storage paths where weights live, and no full copies on laptops or in shared buckets. The threat model resembles code-signing key protection more than ordinary data security, because a single successful exfiltration is unrecoverable.
topics.name: Model Theft
topics.blurb: Weight exfiltration and model extraction through APIs, and what providers disclose about protecting them.

topics.body: The architectural fix is a governed gateway: give the workforce a sanctioned AI access point with logging, data controls, and model choice good enough that the path of least resistance runs through it. Visibility follows adoption; an enterprise that provides the best available tool sees its usage, while an enterprise that bans everything sees nothing and hosts everything.
topics.name: Shadow AI
topics.blurb: Unsanctioned AI use inside organizations: the exposure it creates and how enterprises detect and govern it.

topics.body: Architecturally, assume malware families mutate faster than signatures can chase and let containment carry more weight: segmentation, egress control, and application allow-listing blunt AI-accelerated attacks the same way they blunt human ones, without needing to recognize the specific artifact first.
topics.name: AI-enabled Malware
topics.blurb: What is documented, by primary sources, about AI-assisted malicious code and the vendor and government reporting on it.

topics.body: Phishing-resistant authentication is the control that does not care how good the lure was: hardware-bound passkeys and FIDO2 credentials cannot be phished into a fake login page, which makes them the architectural answer to a threat that has stopped being detectable by reading. Where the lure leads to credential entry, the credential should be one that entry cannot compromise.
topics.name: AI Phishing and Social Engineering
topics.blurb: How generated text and voice change phishing at scale, per published incident and vendor reporting.

topics.body: Architecture-layer tooling enforces boundaries: AI gateways centralizing model access with authentication and rate control, guardrail frameworks applying policy to inputs and outputs, sandboxes isolating tool execution, and the identity infrastructure issuing scoped, short-lived credentials to agents. These are the components that turn least-privilege intentions into enforced fact, and they matter more than any detection layer because they hold even when detection misses.
topics.name: AI Security Tooling
topics.blurb: The defensive tooling landscape, organized by six security domains: Security Governance and Risk Management, Security Operations, Architecture and Engineering, Application and Product Security, Third-Party and Supply Chain Risk, and Data Protection and Privacy.

topics.body: Non-human identities already outnumber human ones in most enterprises, and agents accelerate the ratio: every agent needs credentials, every integration needs a key, and each accumulates access no human formally reviewed. The architecture that scales is the workload-identity discipline applied to agents, short-lived credentials issued per task rather than standing keys, delegation chains that carry the originating user's authority rather than a service account's omnibus permissions, and revocation that actually propagates when an agent is retired, compromised, or simply forgotten.
topics.name: Agent and Non-Human Identity
topics.blurb: The explosion of machine identities: agent credentials, delegated authority, revocation, and the lateral movement paths nobody is watching.

topics.body: Agent security is envelope design: machine-enforced limits on what an agent can spend, touch, and trigger, circuit breakers that halt execution when behavior exits the envelope, and trust boundaries between agents so that one compromised or confused agent cannot instruct another into escalation. Humans are too slow to supervise machine-speed loops in real time, so the envelope has to be enforced by machinery, with the protocol-level guidance for tool ecosystems, including MCP's security best practices, defining where those boundaries sit.
topics.name: AI Agent Security
topics.blurb: Agent kill chains, cascading multi-agent failure, circuit breakers, agent-to-agent trust boundaries, and runtime supervision of autonomous systems.

topics.body: The SOC's own AI is a target inside the defense: alert content, log fields, and ticket text are attacker-writable, which makes the copilot readable by the adversary through the very data it analyzes. Instrumenting the watcher, logging its inputs and recommendations, constraining what it can execute, and red-teaming it with poisoned telemetry, applies the program's own standards to its most privileged AI system.
topics.name: AI in Security Operations
topics.blurb: Defending with AI: machine-speed investigation, human supervision models, automation bias, kill-switch protocols, and securing the SOC's own AI.

topics.body: Purpose limitation becomes real when it is enforced in the pipeline: purpose tags that travel with data, retrieval layers that check purpose before serving training or inference jobs, regional routing for cross-border inference where residency rules were written for storage but exposure happens at inference, and retention TTLs on memory and vector stores. The vector store deserves particular attention as a persistence and exfiltration layer, a dense copy of everything embedded, sitting outside most data maps.
topics.name: AI Privacy and Data Protection
topics.blurb: The deletion problem in trained models, inference as data collection, memory sprawl, purpose enforcement, and cross-border inference.

topics.body: Red-team findings that get fixed with a prompt patch return; findings fixed with an architectural change stay fixed. The discipline is routing systemic findings, injection paths, over-broad tool scopes, missing egress controls, into design remediation rather than instruction tweaks, and treating a finding that recurs across model versions as an architecture bug by definition.
topics.name: AI Red Teaming and Adversarial Evaluation
topics.blurb: Continuous adversarial testing of AI systems: methods, benchmarks, disclosure practices, and the evidence that earns expanded autonomy.

topics.body: Architects decide where an AI feature sits and what it can reach, so that a flaw found late is contained rather than systemic. They also design the pipeline itself: isolated build environments, signed artifacts, and a record of which model and prompt produced each generated change.
topics.name: Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC)
topics.blurb: Building security into every phase of how software is planned, written, tested and shipped, and what changes when AI writes the code and AI features ship in the product.

topics.body: Architects build the containment: a distinct identity per agent, sandboxed execution, a gateway for every tool, and separation between the agent that proposes an action and the service that validates and executes it. Least privilege is enforced by the platform, not trusted to the prompt.
topics.name: Agent Development Lifecycle (ADLC) Security
topics.blurb: The security risks of building, deploying and running autonomous AI agents: tool and MCP bridges, prompt attacks on dynamic input, agent-made supply chain risk, and failures at machine speed.

program.body: Zero trust has to be restated for a caller that can be talked into things. Never trust the model's account of who it is acting for; derive it from the token. Never trust its account of what it needs; derive it from the task. Never let the model hold a credential; the enforcement layer holds it. Volume IX maps this onto the published architecture: NIST SP 800-207's policy decision point, split into policy engine and policy administrator, and its policy enforcement point sit directly onto agent infrastructure, and the requirement that every subject be evaluated, not only the human ones, is what brings machine identities inside the perimeter of the standard. Control frameworks are meeting it from the other side, with the Cloud Security Alliance's AI Controls Matrix carrying 247 control objectives across 18 domains.
program.name: Zero Trust for ML Pipelines

program.body: Confidential computing runs the model, prompt and context in hardware that even the infrastructure operator cannot inspect. Volume IX shows what that now looks like on shared accelerators: a published design hosts many agents inside a single confidential virtual machine with nested isolation, establishes trust between principals through differential attestation, and records provenance for every external interaction, implemented on AMD SEV-SNP and NVIDIA H100 hardware. The pattern matters more than the product, because the workload's secrets are released only after the platform proves what it is running. What an enclave still does not do is make a model less persuadable: a model inside one is exactly as open to prompt injection as a model outside it, and side channels have been shown to leak prompts from inside a confidential environment.
program.name: Secure Enclaves

program.body: Least privilege, scope, expiry and delegation are forty years old and still work; what is new is the scale and the speed. Volume IX's worked case counted a little over nine thousand machine identities across two clouds, a count that took three weeks, and in the week after it finished the estate created about six hundred new identities and retired about four hundred, almost none by a human hand, because a pipeline issues short lived credentials for every build. A periodic inventory cannot hold that; the volume replaces it with a register maintained by the systems that issue the identities, with a lifecycle standard attached, and every privileged non-human identity carrying a named human owner and a ratified scope.

program.body: Segmentation for AI starts with knowing what is talking to models, and Volume IX reframes the whole network layer around agent traffic, where the harmful request and the routine one are the same shape. That covers segmentation and egress, TLS inspection, service mesh identity, the metadata endpoint, DNS, and key design, each treated as a control on machine callers rather than on users. Inside the serving stack, isolation is a tested requirement rather than a diagram: the volume's Isolation Tier Table records what level of separation each workload actually has, and research on multi-tenant serving has shown a shared cache can let one tenant reconstruct another's prompts.

program.body: The gateway is where AI policy is enforced, and two points decide whether it works. First, limits must be enforced outside the model: every production agent above the lowest authority tier gets hard limits on transaction value, API call volume, execution time, data read and written, delegation depth, external destinations and retries, and when one is breached the agent stops rather than degrading. Second, ownership: security teams operate the gateway, but what it blocks, flags and passes is often a privacy decision, so the policy configuration belongs to the function whose decision it encodes. The gateway access log doubles as the inventory of who is calling which model.

program.body: A vector store is a data store, whatever the architecture diagram calls it. Volume IX's worked case is the ordinary one: a data scientist built one from a notebook during a three week experiment, it lived in a managed database service inside a monitored subscription, and the posture tool reported it correctly as a database with encryption at rest. What the tool could not report was that its contents were regulated personal information, because nothing in the resource's configuration said so and nobody had tagged it, since nobody thought of it as a copy of the data. Discovery for the AI layer has to read what is inside embeddings, prompt logs, agent memory and retrieval corpora, not just what the resource is labelled.

program.body: Keys decide who can read. Managed services encrypt with envelope encryption, where a data key encrypts the data and is itself encrypted under a key the customer defines, and access runs through key policies, identity policies and grants. Grants are the loose end: services create them on a customer's behalf and retire them when a task completes, which makes them useful and easy to lose track of. Encryption also decides what deletion can achieve. Cryptographic erase is a purge technique under NIST SP 800-88 Revision 2, and it works only where the data was encrypted as it was stored, from the start, so a store that was never encrypted cannot be erased that way however good the key management is.

program.body: The estate now includes hardware the organisation owns and does not touch. Volume IX's physical estate chapter opens with a GPU server in a colocation cage reporting a fault on a Tuesday night: the platform team raised a remote hands ticket, a technician nobody had met swapped the compute tray, boxed the failed one and shipped it to the manufacturer under warranty, and the ticket closed in ninety minutes with everyone following the process. The questions that follow are the controls: what was on that tray, who handled it, what proves it was sanitised, and what firmware runs beneath it all. The volume's Physical Estate Responsibility Map and Facility Evidence Checklist are where those answers are recorded.

program.body: For AI, resilience is mostly a question of blast radius, and Volume IX gives it a calculator rather than a maturity level: what an application or agent can reach and change, bounded before deployment. The compute chapter covers the parts an ordinary continuity plan misses, including container escapes that need only an image, accelerator sharing modes that differ from hardware isolation, and recovery when retraining a model takes weeks rather than restoring from a backup in hours. Permission design is still the largest single driver: an application acting on one service account holding every permission any user might need can be made, by one injected instruction, to use all of it.

program.scope: Designing AI infrastructure to withstand denial of service.

program.body: An audit trail for AI has to answer the regulator's question: who made this call? For a supervised autonomous action that means the machine's recommendation, the evidence it used, the reviewer who received it, the checks they ran, the decision and the timestamp of every step. For AI products, the same standard applies to the threat model and the tests: every change to the ledger of risks produces a delta, every delta closes with a recorded re-verification, and every model version change has a closed delta before the release that carried it. That turns "the threat model is current" from an assertion into a sentence an auditor can actually write.
